speaker: Jim Keller
title: Jim Keller: Moore's Law, Microprocessors, and First Principles (#70)
question: In modern CPU design, how much parallelism can hardware actually extract from typical sequential software?
guest: About 10x. If you execute a program in order, you get what's called cycles per instruction, and it would be about three cycles per instruction because of the latency of the operations and stuff. A modern computer executes it at like 0.2 to 0.25 cycles per instruction, so today we find about 10x. There are two things behind that. One is the found parallelism in the narrative. The other is the predictability of the narrative. Certain operations do a bunch of calculations and say if greater than one, do this, else do that. That decision is predicted in modern computers to high ninety percent accuracy. Branches happen a lot—imagine you have a decision to make every six instructions, which is about the average. If you want to fetch five hundred instructions, figure out the dependency graph, and execute them all in parallel—say you fetch six hundred instructions and there's a branch every six—you have to predict ninety-nine out of a hundred branches correctly for that window to be effective.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Modest amounts: in practice, modern out-of-order cores sustain roughly 2–4 instructions per cycle on typical sequential integer code, even though they are built much wider than that.

Today's high-end cores (Apple's M-series, AMD Zen 5, Intel's Lion Cove) can decode and dispatch 8–10 instructions per cycle and keep reorder windows of 500–900+ instructions. Yet measured IPC on general-purpose workloads like SPECint usually lands around 2–4, sometimes below 1 for pointer-chasing, cache-missing code, and higher (5–6+) for regular, loop-heavy numeric code.

The gap comes from three limits: branch mispredictions, which cap how far ahead the core can usefully speculate; memory latency and cache misses, which stall dependent chains; and true data dependencies, which form serial chains no hardware can reorder.

Classic limit studies (Wall, 1991; Lam and Wilson, 1992) frame this well: with realistic prediction and window sizes, available parallelism is about 4–10; with perfect branch prediction and unlimited windows, it rises to tens or hundreds. So the parallelism exists in theory, but hardware captures only a small slice, with diminishing returns per added transistor — which is why the industry turned to multicore and SIMD.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
In modern high-performance CPUs, hardware typically extracts about 1.5 to 4 instructions per cycle (IPC) on average from general-purpose sequential software, even though flagship superscalar cores can decode and issue 6 to 10 instructions simultaneously. Processors uncover this instruction-level parallelism dynamically through deep out-of-order execution windows that inspect hundreds of in-flight instructions at once, supported by register renaming, aggressive branch prediction, and memory prefetching.

Actual parallelism varies significantly by workload: predictable, compute-dense code can sustain 5 or 6 IPC, whereas pointer-chasing applications like compilers or databases often drop near or below 1 IPC. Three fundamental bottlenecks enforce this ceiling. First, true data dependencies serialize calculations that require prior results. Second, branches occur roughly every five to ten instructions, so even 99% prediction accuracy still triggers frequent pipeline flushes that bound useful speculative lookahead. Third, main-memory cache misses stall execution for hundreds of cycles. Because wider out-of-order hardware yields steep diminishing returns against these limits, further performance scaling relies on explicit multicore and SIMD parallelism.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Typical sequential software gets about 2 to 4 instructions per cycle (IPC) from modern hardware. That holds even though the widest cores are built to handle 8 to 10 instructions per cycle.

Today's top out-of-order cores, such as Apple's M-series, AMD Zen 5 and Intel Lion Cove, decode 6 to 10 instructions per cycle. They track roughly 500 to 600+ instructions in flight and use very accurate branch predictors. Integer benchmarks like SPECint usually run at about 2 to 3 IPC on these chips. Friendly loops can reach 4 to 6. Large server workloads such as databases and web services often stay below 1 IPC because they keep missing in the cache and branch predictor.

Theory allows much more. Limit studies like David Wall's 1991 "Limits of Instruction-Level Parallelism" found that idealized machines could reach tens to hundreds of IPC. Realistic designs reached only about 5 to 7, held back by data dependencies, branch mispredictions, memory latency and the cost of finding independent work. Each extra step of width or window size gives less benefit and costs more power and area. So single-thread performance now grows only modestly each year, and big gains need explicit parallelism: multiple cores, SIMD or accelerators.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
On typical sequential general-purpose software, modern out-of-order CPUs can usually sustain only about 1.5 to 3 instructions per clock cycle (IPC), even though flagship cores today can decode and issue 6 to 10 instructions per cycle and track hundreds of instructions in flight. While highly regular, compute-heavy loops can briefly push above 4 to 6 IPC, ordinary control- and pointer-heavy code hits hard fundamental limits.

True data dependencies—where each instruction needs the result of the previous one, especially during pointer chasing—form serial chains that no hardware scheduler can parallelize. Control flow compounds the problem: branches occur roughly every five to seven instructions, so even 98–99% branch prediction accuracy limits how far ahead speculative execution can reliably extract independent work. Finally, cache misses and memory latency frequently stall execution before the reorder buffer can uncover enough independent operations. Because hardware faces steep diminishing returns trying to push instruction-level parallelism further, modern performance scaling relies primarily on explicit parallelism like multiple cores, SIMD vectorization, and specialized accelerators.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Modern out-of-order CPUs can usually extract enough instruction-level parallelism from ordinary sequential code to retire about **1–4 instructions per clock cycle per core**. That’s a rough range. Code that frequently waits on memory can average below one, while stretches of independent arithmetic can run near the core’s peak throughput.

The CPU looks ahead and executes independent instructions as soon as their inputs are ready. A chain of instructions that each need the previous result still has to run in order, and cache misses and branch mispredictions can leave parts of the core idle. Even a core that can retire eight instructions in one cycle may average only two or three over a whole program. SIMD and multiple threads can provide more parallelism when the workload can use them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A modern high-performance CPU can often execute a few instructions per clock cycle from one thread. Roughly 1–4 retired instructions per cycle is a useful ballpark for ordinary scalar code, though the result depends on the processor, instruction set, and workload.

The CPU looks ahead in the instruction stream, predicts branches, and executes independent instructions while earlier ones are still in flight. It can track hundreds of instructions at once, but that doesn’t mean it finishes hundreds per cycle. A loop that sums several independent arrays can keep multiple execution units busy. A loop that follows a linked list has much less parallelism because each load must produce the address for the next one.

That estimate describes instruction-level parallelism within one core. SIMD instructions can process several data elements per instruction, and using additional cores generally requires the software or compiler to expose independent work.
